author: Autodesk
description: This graph provides an easy way to turn arbitrary meshes into a cloud-like volume.  Volumes can also be cached to disk as .vdb files.
documentation:
## Ragged Cloud

### Description

This graph shows you how to create a ragged cloud from an input geometry. Working with volumes, fields and noise, you can create a cloud from any base geometry you like quickly and with a consistent looking result.  Starting from any geometry, the graph first displaces the geo with noise in one direction (y) - this allows us to "flatten" the bottom of the cloud.  Once the geometry is displaced, it is converted to a volume, then a voxel field and an iterative `advect_field` is performed on it.  What this means is that it is run through a loop which advects the volume to finer and finer noise details as the loop goes on. Optionally, this displaced level set can be cached for speed if one needs to make any changes downstream in the graph. The level set is then converted to a fog volume. Lastly, a material is assigned and we output a cloud!

### Inputs, Controls & Outputs

The graph asks you to input a geometry and a detail size (resolution) for the fog volume.

Inside the iterate advection loop are several settings that will control the magnitude and strength of the advection.  These are in the "advection settings" and "noise settings" on the node.  they are explained in full inside the iteration node.

You can adjust the output fog volume with an fCurve field input on the "convert sdf to fog" compound.

An Arnold standard volume material is the final step before display, all the material settings can be adjusted.

### Best Practices and Tips

* Unlike simulations, working at a lower resolution in a procedural volume setup like this has a much smaller effect on the final result.  To get your details started it is recommended to set your `detail_size` input to a higher number until you are happy with the results, then make it smaller for final output at the desired resolution.

* The Arnold standard volume material has a large effect on your final render. The example includes dual scattering and attempts to emulate a real cloud. Tweak the material as needed since this is a starting point.

* Work efficiently. We have included a cache in the example so that you can write the volume to disk before making any final tweaks to the shader.  This will speed up your workflow.

_notes.text:
This compound will generate the volume that the cloud is sourced from.

Dive inside for details.
This controls the resolution of the entire simulation, you can make this value bigger to get a faster, less accurate volume for testing purposes.

An iterate loop that adds details to the volume output from the source_volume compound.
Dive inside for details.
The file_cache compound can be used to save the volume data to disk. This can be helpful when working with high resolution clouds where reading the data from disk is quicker than regenerating it.

Converting the level set volume back into a fog volume for the cloud.
Dive in for details.

This uses the volume scope to build diagnostics.
Dive in for details.
Switch the condition to 'True' to use a smaller voxel size and create a higher resolution cloud
Define a volume material that has anisotropic scatter to create a realistic looking cloud.
The descend compound uses math to generate a gradually decreasing number over the iterations.  Dive in for more info.

To get a noise field to change, we use the time input.  This section replaces a time input with the loop iterations.  They are converted to floats, then multiplied by a value and converted to a scalar field to drive changes on the noise fields every time around the loop.

Because fields are much much faster than volumes in calculation, here we generate a noise field using 2 fractal fields.  Fractal Noise (2d) and fractal turbulence (3d).  Because our noise field is going to be used to advect our volume every iteration, it needs to be a 3d field.  Here we are using our generated seed and our iteration-based scalar field to generate the fields.
Here we are adding a small 2d offset to the fractal noise field - the 2d part of our calculations.
We then multiply the 3d field by the 2d field, basically using our 2d fields as a magnitude multiplier for the 3d one
The resulting field is then clamped. This helps establish a flat base of the cloud.
Here we are converting the volume coming in to a field.  We do this by using the signed distance of the incoming volume.
We calculate the bounding box of the volume and use it as a bounds object for the output so that we are not performing calculations unnecessarily.
advect_field advects our signed distance field along a velocity field for the length specified by the time step.  This has the effect of "displacing" the field.

Here is where we are taking the reults of all the field calculations and converting it back into a volume.  This is still a level set volume at this stage.  As you can see on the output, this is the object the loop is iterating over (port feedback).  This means that the result of this iteration is used for the input of the next iteration.
The "base" value is current iteration of the loop, converted to float, here an exponent is applied to it.
A constant value is added to the rseult of the power compound.
The resulting value is divided from one, returning the reciprocal value.
The entire result is then scaled by the "scale" input
This math generates a decreasing value based on the current iteration of the loop.  This means that for every time you go around the loop, this value gets smaller and smaller.
The "base" value is current iteration of the loop, converted to float, here an exponent is applied to it.
A constant value is added to the result of the power compound.
The resulting value is divided from one, returning the reciprocal value.
The entire result is then scaled by the "scale" input
This math generates a decreasing value based on the current iteration of the loop.  This means that for every time you go around the loop, this value gets smaller and smaller.

While one can simply convert to a level set, using an fcurve to to define the conversion of a  signed distance to a fog density can allow for art direction.
Do note that the curve can be sensitive to small value changes and produce a different look easily.
This input and compound will generate a random seed that is used in the graph to control displacements.  The inputs allow you to vary the seed per frame and set a master seed for the whole graph.
This generates and scales the geometry.  Feel free to replace `create_mesh_sphere` with any geo you wish to use and adjust the scale.
This displaces geometry based on the y-position of the incoming points.  more detail inside.
We output the volume as the basis of the cloud, and the seed for further use.

This section creates and controls the volume we will be turning into our cloud.  It converts the displaced mesh from the last section into a volume. The resolution affects the look and the speed of the graph.

_backdrops.title: Displace the mesh points to vary the base shape to look more cloud-like

_notes.text: This will constrain the bounds of the volume display to a slice across the middle, or leave them unconstrained to view the whole volume.
